title: Ladies First
synopsis: Your small-town women's coalition has won a council seat. The seat is yours. The town is split. The first session is Monday and the agenda includes a budget you've been fighting for two years.

nodes.text: You win by 41 votes. Your mom cries. Your kid, eleven, is asleep on the couch. The coalition is in your living room making absurdly bad coffee. Choose “Thank the coalition publicly tonight” and The Mayor's Call comes into view; choose “Save the thank-yous for Monday” and the road bends toward Your Mother.

choices.consequence: You choose to thank the coalition publicly tonight. It opens the route to The Mayor's Call, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.
You choose to save the thank-yous for Monday. It opens the route to Your Mother, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: The mayor, who endorsed your opponent, calls to congratulate you. He uses your first name without permission. He invites you to coffee. You realize he is, professionally, already negotiating. The paths divide here: “Accept the coffee” leads into Monday Session, while “Decline politely” makes The Coalition the next reckoning.

choices.consequence: You commit to accept the coffee. By Monday Session, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.
You commit to decline politely. By The Coalition, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Your mother, who once ran for the same seat and lost twice, makes you sit on the porch with her. 'They will try to make you a kind of woman they can manage,' she says.

choices.text: Ask her how she avoided that
choices.consequence: You ask her how she avoided that. The decision moves you toward Monday Session and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Ask her what she thought she should have done differently
choices.consequence: You ask her what she thought she should have done differently. The decision moves you toward The Coalition and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: You sit at the council table for the first time. There are six of you. You are the only woman. The first item is, unbelievably, the budget you've been pushing for two years. The paths divide here: “Lead with the budget” leads into The Budget Vote, while “Read the room first” makes Your Kid's Questions the next reckoning.

choices.consequence: You commit to lead with the budget. By The Budget Vote, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.
You commit to read the room first. By Your Kid's Questions, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Wednesday night meeting at the church basement. Three new members. Two are nervous. One is, you can tell, already angling to be the next candidate. You realize you have to be a leader the coalition wants to follow.

choices.text: Make space for the ambitious one
choices.consequence: You choose to make space for the ambitious one. It opens the route to The Budget Vote, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Set firm expectations for the coalition
choices.consequence: You choose to set firm expectations for the coalition. It opens the route to Your Kid's Questions, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: The vote is three to three. You sit with it for a long second. The deciding vote is, of course, an unexpected councilman who, you realize, is voting his conscience for the first time. The distance between The Editorial and The Town Hall begins with the choice between “Thank him publicly after” and “Thank him privately and protect him.”

choices.consequence: You commit to thank him publicly after. By The Editorial, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

choices.text: Thank him privately and protect him
choices.consequence: You commit to thank him privately and protect him. By The Town Hall, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Your kid, eleven, asks you, with great seriousness, what your job is now. You think for a long minute. The distance between The Editorial and The Town Hall begins with the choice between “Tell her exactly that” and “Give her the kid-version.”

choices.consequence: You tell her exactly that. The decision moves you toward The Editorial and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.
You commit to give her the kid-version. By The Town Hall, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: The local paper writes an editorial about your first vote. It is, mostly, generous. It is, in one paragraph, condescending. You realize the editor is, separately, going to be your neighbor for a long time.

choices.text: Respond to the editorial in a letter
choices.consequence: You commit to respond to the editorial in a letter. By The Difficult Vote, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

choices.text: Don't respond; let the work speak
choices.consequence: You choose to don't respond; let the work speak. It opens the route to The Quiet Win, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: Your first town hall as a councilmember. The room is louder than the council chamber. A man in the back yells about your funding decision. A woman near the front cries because of it. The distance between The Difficult Vote and The Quiet Win begins with the choice between “Address the man first” and “Address the woman first.”

choices.consequence: You choose to address the man first. It opens the route to The Difficult Vote, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.
You commit to address the woman first. By The Quiet Win, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: Three months in. A vote on whether to fund a new library or repair the old highway bridge. The county will subsidize either, not both. You can guess which option the men will pick. “Push for the library” opens the route to The Re-Election Year. “Push for the bridge” changes the terms and carries you toward The Daughter Watching.

choices.consequence: You push for the library. The decision moves you toward The Re-Election Year and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.
You commit to push for the bridge. By The Daughter Watching, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: You and the unexpected councilman start meeting for breakfast. You don't agree on much. You agree on the budget for the food pantry. The breakfasts become, in their way, the actual government. “Codify the alliance” draws you toward The Re-Election Year; “Keep it informal” leaves The Daughter Watching waiting on the other side.

choices.consequence: You choose to codify the alliance. It opens the route to The Re-Election Year, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.
You keep it informal. The decision moves you toward The Daughter Watching and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: Two years pass. Your re-election campaign is, mercifully, less of a fight than the first. You win by 312 votes. The coalition has, in your absence, doubled. “Run for mayor next cycle” draws you toward Mayor; “Stay on the council and build” leaves Your Library Wins waiting on the other side.

choices.consequence: You commit to run for mayor next cycle. By Mayor, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

choices.text: Stay on the council and build
choices.consequence: You stay on the council and build. The decision moves you toward Your Library Wins and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: Your daughter, thirteen now, sits in on a council meeting and watches you for two hours. Afterward she says, 'I want to do that.' You realize you have, accidentally, started a small generational thing. The distance between Mayor and Your Library Wins begins with the choice between “Mentor her properly” and “Let her find her own version.”

choices.consequence: You mentor her properly. The decision moves you toward Mayor and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Let her find her own version
choices.consequence: You let her find her own version. The decision moves you toward Your Library Wins and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: You run for mayor. The town is, again, split. You win, again, narrowly. Your mother is in the audience at the swearing-in, in a dress she's owned since 1987. She doesn't cry. Her dress, she says, is too good.

choices.text: Make 'small town, big work' your platform
choices.consequence: You commit to make 'small town, big work' your platform. By First Hundred Days, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.
You choose to just do the work quietly. It opens the route to First Hundred Days, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: The library opens, eventually. There is a small plaque with your name and three other names. Your daughter cuts the ribbon because you insisted. The whole coalition is in the front row. So is your mother.

choices.text: Use the library opening for the next campaign
choices.consequence: You choose to use the library opening for the next campaign. It opens the route to The County Conference, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.
You choose to just celebrate the library. It opens the route to The County Conference, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: The first hundred days are paperwork, parking, ordinances. Glamorous it is not. You realize, slowly, that being mayor is mostly the work of returning calls. You return them. You cannot avoid The Veto; you can only decide whether “Keep returning every call personally” or “Hire a chief of staff” defines the person who reaches it.

choices.consequence: You keep returning every call personally. The decision moves you toward The Veto and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.
You choose to hire a chief of staff. It opens the route to The Veto, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: You attend a county-wide conference of small-town officials. Half of them are women now. Five years ago, two of them were. You realize you have, accidentally, been part of a shift. The Regional Coalition Meeting comes either way; its meaning changes with the difference between “Take the lead on a regional coalition” and “Stay focused on your own town.”

choices.text: Take the lead on a regional coalition
choices.consequence: You choose to take the lead on a regional coalition. It opens the route to The Regional Coalition Meeting, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

choices.text: Stay focused on your own town
choices.consequence: You choose to stay focused on your own town. It opens the route to The Regional Coalition Meeting, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: Your first veto. The bill is, on balance, bad. The council member who proposed it is, separately, a friend's husband. You veto it. You call the friend the same night. The friendship survives. The friendship is, briefly, the work.

choices.consequence: You choose to be principled and friendly always. It opens the route to Re-Election Eve, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.
You accept some friendships will fray. The decision moves you toward Re-Election Eve and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: You convene a coalition of nine towns. The first meeting is awkward. The second is, surprisingly, productive. By the third you are voted, against your wishes, the chair. Re-Election Eve is already waiting. What changes is whether “Accept the chair” or “Decline; nominate someone better suited” is the instinct you carry into it.

choices.consequence: You choose to accept the chair. It opens the route to Re-Election Eve, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.
You decline; nominate someone better suited. The decision moves you toward Re-Election Eve and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: Eve of the re-election. The kitchen table, again, late. Your mother, in town for it, has made tea. Your daughter, fifteen, is writing your closing remarks for you. You realize the politics has, finally, become a family practice.

choices.text: Run again with the bigger 'small town' frame
choices.consequence: You run again with the bigger 'small town' frame. The decision moves you toward Mayor for Two Terms and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

choices.text: Run again on quiet, careful substance
choices.consequence: You choose to run again on quiet, careful substance. It opens the route to Councilwoman, Quietly, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: You serve two terms as mayor and shape, slowly, a town that looks like the town you wanted to grow up in. Your daughter, fifteen, runs for student council and wins. Your mother, in her late seventies, retires into proudly criticizing the new mayor.

You stay on the council. You build, quietly, slowly, decisively. People stop being surprised that a woman has the seat. Your kid grows up in a town that is, in small ways, kinder. That, you realize, was always the point.
